text.title: Statistical Significance: Basics Core Rules
text.summary: 13 testable rules every application of `Statistical Significance: Basics` must enforce. Each rule pairs a binary check with a sourced rationale. Null hypothesis, p-value, alpha, power, confidence intervals, and the Type I/II error trade-off.

section.title: Background
section.p: Frequentist p-values say "if H0 is true, how likely is this data?" Bayesian posteriors say "given this data, how likely is B better?" For teams that want intuitive probability statements, Bayesian A/B testing is a valid alternative but requires prior assumptions.

rule.statement: Alpha (significance level) MUST be set before the test starts. Standard alpha = 0.05 unless multi-test correction applies.
rule.rationale: Setting alpha post-hoc is a fishing license. Pre-commit alpha = pre-commit to honest stopping rule.

rule.statement: Sample size per arm MUST come from power analysis (baseline rate + MDE + alpha + 80% power). Hand-wave sample sizes forbidden.
rule.rationale: Without power analysis, an inconclusive test could mean 'no effect' or 'too small to detect'. Power analysis tells you what sample size is honest for the question.

rule.statement: Null + alternative hypothesis MUST be written out before the test (H0: control = treatment; H1: control != treatment OR pre-registered direction).
rule.rationale: Vague hypothesis = vague test = post-hoc rationalization. Formal H0 + H1 keeps the test honest.

rule.statement: Test design MUST acknowledge Type I (alpha, false-positive) vs Type II (1-power, false-negative) tradeoff. Default 80% power = 20% Type II rate.

rationale.source: Cohen 1988; Practical Statistics for Data Scientists

rule.rationale: Type II error is the silent killer — you keep the bad treatment because the test was too small to see the effect. Explicit acknowledgment forces honest sample-size discussion.

rule.statement: Default frequentist test MUST not peek + stop. If peeking required, use sequential testing (mSPRT, alpha-spending, Bayesian) — declared in pre-test brief.

rationale.source: Sequential testing literature; Berman / Optimizely guides

rule.rationale: Peeking inflates actual alpha. The fix is either fixed-horizon (no peeking) or explicit sequential method. Mixing the two = false positives.

rule.statement: State H0 (no difference) and H1 (difference exists) before collecting any data.
rule.rationale: Post-hoc hypothesis selection inflates false positive rates; the null hypothesis is the default claim the test must disprove.

rule.statement: Set alpha = 0.05 before launch; reject H0 only when p-value is strictly less than alpha.
rule.rationale: Alpha defines acceptable false positive rate. p-value is the probability of seeing this result (or more extreme) if H0 were true — not the probability that B is better.

rule.statement: Target 80% power; calculate required sample size from baseline rate, MDE, alpha, and power before starting.
rule.rationale: 80% power means a 20% chance of missing a real effect (Type II error). Running underpowered tests wastes traffic and produces untrustworthy null results.

rule.statement: Report the 95% CI for the difference alongside p-value; do not ship a result where the CI lower bound is economically irrelevant.
rule.rationale: A significant p-value with CI [0.01%, 4%] is statistically real but the lower bound may not justify shipping costs. CI width reflects data quantity — wider = need more data.

rule.statement: Alpha controls Type I error (false positive); power controls Type II error (false negative) — tune both for the business cost of each mistake.
rule.rationale: Shipping a bad change (Type I) is costly in high-traffic funnels. Missing a real improvement (Type II) is costly when testing is expensive. High-stakes tests warrant alpha=0.01 or power=90%.

rule.statement: Use a two-proportion z-test for conversion rate comparisons; always two-tailed unless a regression would never be shipped.
rule.rationale: Two-tailed tests do not assume the direction of the effect, preventing directional bias that inflates Type I error for the expected direction.

rule.statement: Calculate n per variant as ceil(16 * p * (1-p) / MDE^2) at 95% confidence / 80% power; use the exact statsmodels formula for asymmetric splits.
rule.rationale: The simplified formula (16 * p(1-p)/MDE^2) is accurate for 50/50 splits. Asymmetric traffic splits require the full formula via NormalIndPower().solve_power().

rule.statement: When preconditions in Applies If fail OR any item in Skip If triggers, do not run this methodology. Document the skip rationale in the artefact's parent log.
rule.rationale: Misapplied methodologies are worse than no methodology — they consume review cycles and produce false confidence.
